section: Prerequisites / You will learn / Why this matters
question: What is '3D parallelism' in frontier-model training?
options: Running three independent training runs on separate clusters and averaging their weights
Splitting a model's layers across exactly three GPUs, one third of the depth on each device
Combining data, tensor and pipeline parallelism at the same time
Sharding parameters, gradients and optimizer state at once, as in ZeRO stage 3
explanation: 3D parallelism combines data parallelism (split the data), tensor parallelism (split within layers), and pipeline parallelism (split across layers). Expert parallelism is added on top for Mixture-of-Experts models. Sharding all three model-state buckets is ZeRO-3, a different idea.

section: Prerequisites / You will learn / Why this matters
question: Why is it useful to know what each parallelism axis splits and what it costs in communication?
options: It determines the model's final accuracy, since each axis changes the loss curve
It lets you read a large-model training report and plan a training layout
It replaces scaling laws, since the layout alone fixes the optimal model size
It lets you pick a layout that avoids inter-device communication entirely
explanation: Frontier runs use several parallelism axes at once, each with its own communication pattern and cost. Knowing them lets you interpret the configuration in a training report and map axes to hardware when planning one. Parallelism does not change what the model learns.

question: A tensor-parallel example is simulated in one process by computing each device's partial result with NumPy and summing them. What does it reproduce, and what does it not?
options: It reproduces the all-reduce's numbers, not the real gain of fitting or speeding up a big layer
It reproduces the real multi-GPU speedup, but not the exact numbers that an all-reduce would produce
It reproduces both the all-reduce's numbers and the per-device memory savings of the split
It reproduces neither the numbers nor the memory savings, since NumPy has no collectives
explanation: Summing per-device partials in one process gives exactly the output an all-reduce would produce. But the point of real tensor parallelism, fitting a layer that does not fit on one device and computing it faster, can only be shown on real multi-device hardware.

section: 1. When data parallelism and ZeRO run out
question: What assumption do data parallelism and ZeRO/FSDP share that breaks for the largest models?
options: That the full training dataset fits in each node's CPU memory for shuffling
That a single device can, at least momentarily, hold and compute one full layer
That all GPUs sit on one machine and share a single NVLink switch fabric
That the optimizer is plain SGD, so no per-parameter state ever needs to be stored
explanation: Data parallelism replicates the model, and ZeRO/FSDP gather each layer's full weights before computing it. Both assume one device can hold and compute one layer. When a layer's weights or activations are too large, the model itself must be split across devices.

section: 1. When data parallelism and ZeRO run out
question: Which description matches tensor parallelism?
options: Splitting one operation such as a matmul so each device holds part of the weight and output
Assigning a contiguous block of layers to each device and passing activations to the next one
Placing different MoE experts on different devices and routing tokens to their owners
Giving each device a different shard of the training data and averaging the gradients
explanation: Tensor parallelism splits within a layer, across the width of a matmul. Assigning layer ranges is pipeline parallelism, placing experts is expert parallelism, and sharding the data is data parallelism.

section: 1. When data parallelism and ZeRO run out
question: Which description matches pipeline parallelism?
options: Each device holds a column slice of every weight matrix and all-reduces outputs
Each device holds a contiguous range of layers and passes activations to the next
Each device holds a subset of the MoE experts and receives tokens via all-to-all
Each device holds a slice of the token positions and exchanges keys and values for attention
explanation: Pipeline parallelism splits the layer stack (depth) across devices. Each stage computes its layers and sends activations forward, while backward flows in reverse. Slicing every weight matrix is tensor parallelism and slicing token positions is sequence parallelism.

section: 1. When data parallelism and ZeRO run out
question: Which description matches expert parallelism?
options: Each device computes a column block of every matmul and all-reduces the outputs
Each device holds a contiguous range of layers and forwards its activations to the next device
In an MoE, experts live on different devices and tokens are routed to their expert's device
Each device processes a different data shard and the gradients are all-reduced
explanation: Expert parallelism is specific to MoE models. Experts are distributed across devices, and tokens are sent to the device hosting the expert the router selected. It composes with the other parallelism axes.

section: 1. When data parallelism and ZeRO run out
question: How do data parallelism and ZeRO relate to tensor, pipeline and expert parallelism?
options: They compose on top of all three
They are alternatives that cannot be combined with them
They replace tensor parallelism at large scale
They only work with pipeline parallelism
explanation: Data parallelism and ZeRO split the data and the memory, while tensor, pipeline, and expert parallelism split the model itself. Real runs use them together: model-parallel groups form replicas, and data parallelism or ZeRO runs across replicas.

section: 2. Tensor parallelism: split the matmul (Megatron style)
question: What is the key design goal of the Megatron-LM tensor-parallel split for a Transformer MLP?
options: Removing the nonlinearity between the two matmuls so they fuse into one
Making every device hold the full weight matrices to avoid gathering them
Splitting the two matmuls so they need only one communication between them
Communicating the 4C-wide hidden activations after every matmul in the block
explanation: Megatron chooses how to split the MLP's two weight matrices so that the pair needs only one collective (an all-reduce at the end) per pass. The wide hidden activations never have to be communicated.

section: The column-then-row trick for an MLP
question: In a Transformer MLP Y = ReLU(X A) B, what are A and B?
options: A is the attention score matrix; B is the value projection applied to it
A is the C to 4C up projection; B is the 4C to C down projection
A is the 4C to C down projection; B is the C to 4C up projection
A and B are both C by C matrices, so the hidden width stays at C
explanation: The MLP widens the representation from C to 4C with A, applies an element-wise nonlinearity, and projects back from 4C to C with B. GPT-2 uses GELU rather than ReLU, but the tensor-parallel splitting is identical.

section: The column-then-row trick for an MLP
question: In Megatron's column-parallel split of the MLP's first matmul, why can each device apply the nonlinearity without communication?
options: Because ReLU is linear on its domain, so applying it before or after the sum gives an identical result
Each device computes its own slice of the hidden activations, and the nonlinearity is element-wise
Because each device holds the full 4C-wide hidden activations after an implicit all-gather
Because the nonlinearity is deferred until after the all-reduce that follows the second matmul
explanation: Splitting A by columns means device d computes X A_d, a slice of the hidden activations. An element-wise function like ReLU or GELU needs only each element itself, so it can be applied to the slice locally. That is why the column split is placed before the nonlinearity.

section: The column-then-row trick for an MLP
question: In Megatron's MLP split, how is the second matmul B partitioned, and what does each device produce?
options: Row-parallel: B is split by rows matching the hidden slices; each device gives a full-shape partial
Column-parallel: B is split by columns, so each device produces a disjoint slice of the output columns
Replicated: every device holds all of B and produces the full, correct output without communication
Split by batch: each device holds all of B and produces the outputs for a different subset of tokens
explanation: B is split by rows so device d multiplies its hidden slice by B_d. The result has the full C-wide output shape but contains only that device's contribution. The full output is the sum of these partials.

section: The column-then-row trick for an MLP
question: How does Megatron's tensor-parallel MLP obtain the complete output Y on every device?
options: An all-reduce sums the partial outputs: Y = sum over d of ReLU(X A_d) B_d
An all-gather concatenates each device's output columns into the full width-C Y
Rank 0 gathers every partial, computes Y alone, and broadcasts it to the others
Each device already holds the full Y after the row-parallel matmul, with no communication
explanation: Each device's row-parallel result is a partial contribution to Y. One all-reduce with sum adds them, leaving the full Y on every device. Concatenating would be wrong because the partials overlap in shape rather than covering disjoint columns.

section: The column-then-row trick for an MLP
question: Why is Megatron's column-then-row MLP split bandwidth-thrifty?
options: It avoids all communication in the backward pass, since gradients are computed fully locally per shard
It compresses the weight shards to int8 before sending them, cutting each transfer by four
It communicates only the gradients of the nonlinearity, which are tiny compared with activations
The 4C-wide hidden activations are never sent; only the C-wide output is all-reduced once a pass
explanation: Each device keeps its own hidden slice through the nonlinearity, so the wide intermediate never crosses the network. Only the narrower final output is all-reduced, once in forward and once in backward.

question: A two-device tensor-parallel MLP gives device partial outputs [5, 2] and [5, 9], and the single-device output is [10, 11]. What does this demonstrate?
options: Tensor parallelism introduces a small approximation error that is tolerable in practice for training
Summing the row-parallel partials with an all-reduce exactly reconstructs the single-device output
The partials must be concatenated, not summed, to recover the true single-device output
Each device already computed the full output; the two copies differ only by rounding noise
explanation: The element-wise sum [5+5, 2+9] = [10, 11] matches ReLU(XA)B computed on one device. Tensor parallelism is exact: each device held only half of A and half of B and computed on a hidden slice half as wide.

question: In a two-device tensor-parallel MLP with C = 2 (hidden width 4), what does each device hold and compute?
options: Half of A's columns and half of B's rows, computing on a hidden slice of width 2
All of A and half of B's rows, computing on the full hidden width 4 before splitting
Half of A's rows and half of B's columns, computing on half of the input features
All of A and all of B, computing the full MLP on half of the tokens in the batch
explanation: Device 0 takes columns 1 to 2 of A and rows 1 to 2 of B; device 1 takes columns 3 to 4 and rows 3 to 4. Each computes on a hidden slice of width 2 instead of 4. That is how a matmul too big for one device is split and reassembled with one all-reduce.

question: In a tensor-parallel split of an MLP whose first matmul is A, which slices of A and B must a device hold together?
options: The columns of A and the rows of B that correspond to the same hidden units
Any columns of A and any rows of B, since the all-reduce fixes any mismatch
The rows of A and the columns of B that correspond to the same hidden units
All of A, plus only the rows of B that correspond to its assigned hidden units
explanation: Device d's hidden slice is X A_d for some block of hidden units; its partial output multiplies that slice by the rows of B for the same hidden units. Mismatched slices would multiply the wrong hidden activations by the wrong weights.

section: 2. Tensor parallelism: split the matmul (Megatron style)
question: How is multi-head attention tensor-parallelized in Megatron style?
options: Each device computes all heads on a subset of the key dimensions and concatenates the scores
Each device gets a subset of tokens and all heads, exchanging keys and values with the other devices
Each device runs a subset of heads in full; the output projection is row-parallel, one all-reduce
Attention is replicated on every device and only the MLP block is split column-then-row
explanation: Heads are independent, so splitting by heads is natural: each device computes its heads' QKV projections and attention locally. The output projection is split by rows, and one all-reduce sums the partials. That mirrors the MLP's column-then-row pattern.

section: 2. Tensor parallelism: split the matmul (Megatron style)
question: Why is tensor parallelism normally confined to GPUs within one node over NVLink?
options: Because it only supports up to two GPUs, and nodes typically hold exactly that many
Because NVLink hardware is required to execute a split matmul's partial products
It all-reduces in every layer's forward and backward, making it communication-heavy
Because it communicates only once per step, so cross-node latency would simply be wasted
explanation: Tensor parallelism needs an all-reduce in every layer's forward and backward pass. That traffic is affordable only on the fastest links, typically NVLink within a node. Pipeline and data parallelism, which communicate less often, are used across nodes.

section: 3. Pipeline parallelism: split the layer stack
question: With 4 pipeline stages and 32 layers split evenly, which layers does stage 1 hold?
options: Layers 0 to 7
Layers 8 to 15
Layers 1, 5, 9, ...
Layers 16 to 23
explanation: Pipeline parallelism gives each stage a contiguous range of layers. With 32 layers and 4 stages, stage 0 holds 0 to 7, stage 1 holds 8 to 15, and so on. Forward flows stage 0 to stage 3 and backward flows in reverse.

section: 3. Pipeline parallelism: split the layer stack
question: What memory problem does pipeline parallelism solve?
options: It shards activations along the sequence dimension, so long contexts fit on each device
Each device holds only its slice of the model's depth, so a far deeper model fits
It eliminates the optimizer state, since each stage updates its layers with plain SGD
It shrinks each weight matrix by splitting its columns across the pipeline stages
explanation: By assigning different layers to different devices, each device needs only its layers' parameters and their computation. A model too deep for one device can thus be spread across several. Individual layers are still held whole, unlike tensor parallelism.

question: In naive pipeline parallelism with one batch pushed through, what is the 'pipeline bubble'?
options: Extra memory held by in-flight activations waiting for their backward pass
Idle time while stages wait on others, e.g. stages 1-3 idle while stage 0 computes
A numerical error introduced when activations are cast to pass between devices
The time every stage spends waiting on the optimizer step at the end of each full batch
explanation: When one batch flows through, each stage is busy only while that batch is on it, so most devices are idle most of the time. That wasted time is the bubble. It is the fill and drain time at the ends of the pipe.

question: How does pipeline parallelism reduce the bubble?
options: Add more pipeline stages, so each stage's share of the compute and of the idle time shrinks
Split the batch into m micro-batches fed in a staggered stream so all stages stay busy
Run the optimizer step during the forward pass so that idle stages update their layers
All-reduce the activations between stages so every stage can start at the same time
explanation: Once stage 0 passes micro-batch 1 on, it starts micro-batch 2, and so on, like an assembly line. After a short fill, all stages are busy. Only fill and drain at the ends remain as bubble, which more micro-batches amortize.

question: What is the pipeline bubble fraction for S stages and m micro-batches?
explanation: Filling the pipe takes S-1 slots before the last stage starts, and draining takes another S-1, spread over a schedule of m + S - 1 slots. The bubble fraction is (S-1)/(m+S-1). Increasing m amortizes the fixed fill/drain over more useful work.

question: Why does increasing the number of micro-batches m shrink the pipeline bubble fraction?
options: The S-1 fill/drain overhead is fixed, so more micro-batches spread it over more work
Smaller micro-batches compute proportionally faster than full batches on each stage
With enough micro-batches the pipe never has to drain, so the overhead disappears
Each micro-batch is assigned its own stage, so more of them occupy more stages at once
explanation: The fill and drain overhead depends on the number of stages, not on m. Adding micro-batches adds useful slots in the denominator m + S - 1 while the numerator S-1 stays fixed.

question: With 4 pipeline stages and only 1 micro-batch, what fraction of the hardware time is wasted in the bubble?
explanation: Bubble = (S-1)/(m+S-1) = 3/4 = 0.75 with m = 1. With 8 micro-batches it falls to about 27%, and with 32 to under 9%.

question: Why do more sophisticated pipeline schedules such as GPipe and the interleaved 1F1B of Megatron/DeepSpeed exist?
options: To remove the need for a separate backward pass by fusing it into forward
To avoid micro-batches entirely by pipelining individual layers instead
To shrink the bubble and the activation memory further
To allow tensor parallelism to run efficiently across slow inter-node links
explanation: Plain staggered micro-batching still leaves a bubble and keeps many micro-batches' activations alive. Schedules like GPipe and interleaved one-forward-one-backward (1F1B) reorder work to reduce idle time and how much activation memory is held at once.

question: What rule of thumb relates micro-batches m to pipeline stages S?
options: Use m much larger than S, for example m at least 4S
Use m equal to S, so each stage holds exactly one micro-batch
Use m less than S, so that activation memory stays small
Use m = S - 1, which exactly cancels the fill/drain overhead
explanation: Because the bubble is (S-1)/(m+S-1), m near S wastes a large fraction of the hardware. Using m much larger than S, such as m at least 4S, keeps the bubble small.

question: Why does using many pipeline micro-batches increase activation memory?
options: Each in-flight micro-batch keeps its activations alive until its backward pass
Each micro-batch stores its own full copy of the stage's parameters and gradients
Micro-batch activations are kept in fp64 to avoid error accumulating across stages
Each micro-batch's activations are replicated on every stage of the pipeline
explanation: A micro-batch's forward activations must be retained until its backward pass uses them. The more micro-batches are in flight at once, the more activation memory is held. Schedules like GPipe and 1F1B largely differ in how they manage this.

question: Why does load-balancing layers across pipeline stages matter?
options: Unbalanced stages increase the number of gradient all-reduces each step needs
Unbalanced stages produce wrong gradients, because the slow stage lags a step behind
A stage stalls if its input isn't ready, so an uneven split idles fast stages on slow ones
Load balancing lets each stage drop redundant layers, reducing the model's total parameter count
explanation: A pipeline runs at the pace of its slowest stage. If one stage has more compute, the others wait for it. Assigning layers so each stage has equal compute keeps all stages busy.

section: 4. Sequence / context parallelism and expert parallelism
question: What does sequence (context) parallelism split, and what does it target?
options: The batch dimension B; it targets optimizer state, which grows with the global batch size
The sequence length T; it targets memory growing with T, like attention scores and LayerNorm
The hidden width C; it targets the weight matrices, which are too wide for a single device
The experts; it targets MoE routing tables, which grow with the number of tokens per batch
explanation: Sequence parallelism gives each device a slice of the token positions. It shards the activations that grow with sequence length, which tensor parallelism leaves whole. This is what makes very long context lengths trainable.

section: 4. Sequence / context parallelism and expert parallelism
question: Why does sequence parallelism require communication inside attention?
options: Because experts are placed on different devices and every token must visit all of them
Because LayerNorm needs a global mean over the batch, which spans every device's tokens
Because the optimizer state is split by sequence and must be gathered for each step
Each position's query must still see all keys, which may live on other devices
explanation: Attention mixes information across positions: every query attends over all keys. If token positions are split across devices, each device needs keys and values from the others, so communication across the sequence dimension is required. Sequence parallelism composes with tensor parallelism.

section: 4. Sequence / context parallelism and expert parallelism
question: In an MoE layer, what does the router do?
options: Sends each token to every expert and averages their outputs by learned weights
Sends each token to only one or a few of many expert MLPs
Chooses which GPU runs each token's attention computation for the current layer
Selects which Transformer layers each token skips to save compute at inference
explanation: An MoE layer replaces one MLP with many expert MLPs plus a router. The router picks one or a few experts per token, so each token uses only a small part of the layer's parameters.

section: 4. Sequence / context parallelism and expert parallelism
question: Which collective does expert parallelism use to move tokens to their experts and back?
options: All-gather
All-reduce
All-to-all
Broadcast
explanation: In expert parallelism, every device may have tokens for experts on every other device. An all-to-all lets each device send each of its tokens to the device holding its chosen expert and receive the results back.

section: 4. Sequence / context parallelism and expert parallelism
question: Why can an MoE have a huge total parameter count while each device stores and computes only a small part?
options: MoE parameters are stored in int4, so even a huge expert count fits on each device
Each token uses only a couple of experts, and experts are distributed across devices
Experts share all their weights and differ only in a small per-expert bias vector
Only the router has trainable parameters; the experts are frozen random projections
explanation: Total parameters scale with the number of experts, but each token's forward pass touches only the few experts it was routed to. With experts spread across devices, per-device storage and per-token compute stay small.

question: What is the universal performance trick for every parallelism axis' communication?
options: Route all communication through a single designated GPU per node
Compress every communicated tensor to fp8 before it leaves the device
Run all communication only at the end of the step, after backward finishes
Overlap communication with computation so the network cost hides under compute
explanation: Every axis adds communication. Starting the next matmul or all-gather while the current collective is still in flight hides network time under compute, as with DDP and FSDP. A well-tuned run is bottlenecked by arithmetic, not idle waiting.

question: In a typical 3D-parallel layout, how are the axes mapped to the hardware topology?
options: Tensor within a node, pipeline across a few nodes, data parallelism/ZeRO across the rest
Data parallelism within a node, tensor parallelism across nodes, pipeline across racks
Pipeline within a node, tensor parallelism across all nodes, data parallelism per GPU
All axes on the slowest inter-node links, to leave NVLink bandwidth free for compute
explanation: Tensor parallelism's per-layer all-reduces go on the fastest links (NVLink within a node). Pipeline parallelism sends only activations, so it can cross slower links between a few nodes. Data parallelism or ZeRO, with one gradient all-reduce per step, spans the remaining groups.

question: Which framework is the reference implementation of tensor and sequence parallelism?
options: PyTorch FSDP (Meta AI)
DeepSpeed (Microsoft)
Megatron-LM (NVIDIA)
vLLM (UC Berkeley)
explanation: Megatron-LM implements the column-then-row tensor split, sequence parallelism, and interleaved pipeline schedules. Reach for it when you need to split the model's math across devices.

question: Which framework is home to ZeRO and offers memory features such as ZeRO-Offload?
options: PyTorch FSDP (Meta AI)
Megatron-LM (NVIDIA)
DeepSpeed (Microsoft)
NVIDIA NCCL library
explanation: DeepSpeed provides the ZeRO stages and pipeline parallelism, along with optimizer and memory features like ZeRO-Offload. It is the choice for memory-efficient data parallelism with easy ZeRO stages.

question: What does PyTorch FSDP primarily provide among large-scale training frameworks?
options: Native ZeRO-3-style fully sharded data parallelism with little code, gaining TP support
The reference implementation of sequence and tensor parallelism for Transformer blocks
Pipeline schedules such as interleaved 1F1B, with automatic layer-to-stage balancing
All-to-all expert routing and load-balancing losses for Mixture-of-Experts training
explanation: FSDP is PyTorch's native way to shard a model's parameters, gradients, and optimizer state across data-parallel workers. It increasingly supports tensor parallelism too.

question: In practice, what does an ML engineer usually do with large-scale parallelism frameworks?
options: Avoid parallelism frameworks and scale everything with plain DDP and larger batches
Re-implement the NCCL collectives for each project to match the cluster's topology
Write a custom pipeline schedule and tensor split by hand for every new model
Configure the axes and reason about their memory and communication cost
explanation: Correct production versions of topology-aware collectives, overlapped communication, interleaved pipelines, and all-to-all routing are large systems efforts, which is why Megatron, DeepSpeed, and FSDP exist. Building toy versions makes config options like tensor_parallel_size, pipeline_parallel_size, zero_stage, and num_micro_batches understandable.

question: Which paper introduced the column-then-row tensor-parallel split for the MLP and multi-head attention?
options: Megatron-LM: Training Multi-Billion Parameter Language Models Using Model Parallelism (Shoeybi et al., 2019)
ZeRO: Memory Optimizations Toward Training Trillion Parameter Models (Rajbhandari et al., 2019)
GPipe: Efficient Training of Giant Neural Networks using Pipeline Parallelism (Huang et al., 2019)
Switch Transformers: Scaling to Trillion Parameter Models with Simple and Efficient Sparsity (Fedus et al., 2021)
explanation: Megatron-LM (Shoeybi et al., 2019) introduced the column-then-row tensor-parallel split and showed it scaling to billions of parameters. With ZeRO it is one of the two foundational large-model systems papers.

question: With 32 GPUs, tensor parallelism degree 4, and 4 pipeline stages, how many data-parallel replicas can you run?
explanation: One replica uses tensor size times pipeline size = 4 * 4 = 16 GPUs. 32 / 16 = 2 data-parallel replicas, giving the 3D layout tensor(4) * pipeline(4) * data(2) = 32.

question: In a 3D-parallel layout of tensor(4) x pipeline(4) x data(2), what communication happens each step?
options: Only one all-reduce of gradients across all 32 GPUs, as in plain data parallelism
The 2 replicas all-reduce grads; inside each, TP all-reduces per layer, PP passes activations
Only activations are passed between stages; no all-reduce of any kind occurs during the step
Each GPU broadcasts its weight shard to all 31 others before every forward and backward pass
explanation: Data parallelism across the two replicas needs a gradient all-reduce. Inside a replica, tensor parallelism all-reduces partial outputs on every layer, and pipeline parallelism sends activations forward and gradients backward between stages.

question: With 4 pipeline stages, what is the minimum number of micro-batches to keep the bubble below 10%?
explanation: 3/(m+3) < 0.10 requires m + 3 > 30, so m > 27 and the minimum integer is 28. At m = 28 the bubble is 3/31, about 9.7%.

question: What is the key difference between tensor parallelism and pipeline parallelism?
options: Tensor splits across layers and passes activations; pipeline splits within a layer
Tensor splits within a layer, all-reducing per layer; pipeline splits layers, passing activations
Tensor splits the data batch across devices; pipeline splits the optimizer state across stages
They are two names for the same technique, differing only in which framework implements it
explanation: Tensor parallelism divides a matmul's width across devices and needs per-layer all-reduces. Pipeline parallelism assigns layer ranges to devices and sends activations between them. They solve different fit problems and are usually combined.

question: What happens if tensor parallelism is run across slow inter-node links?
options: It automatically falls back to pipeline parallelism across the slow links
It becomes more accurate, because the slower all-reduce uses higher precision
Its per-layer all-reduces dominate and throughput collapses
Nothing much; tensor parallelism communicates only once per optimizer step
explanation: Tensor parallelism all-reduces on every layer's forward and backward. On slow links that traffic cannot hide under compute, so throughput collapses. Keep it on the fastest interconnect, within a node.

question: What is wrong with running a pipeline with a number of micro-batches close to the number of stages?
options: The stages deadlock waiting on each other's backward passes
The gradients become incorrect because micro-batches overlap
The model no longer fits in memory once the stages fill up
The bubble wastes a large fraction of the hardware
explanation: With m near S, (S-1)/(m+S-1) is large: for example S = 8, m = 8 gives about 47% wasted. Use m much larger than S.

question: A pipeline has 8 stages. What bubble fractions do 8 and 64 micro-batches give?
options: About 88% and about 50%
About 12% and about 1%
About 47% and about 10%
About 47% and about 1%
explanation: (S-1)/(m+S-1) with S = 8: m = 8 gives 7/15, about 0.467; m = 64 gives 7/71, about 0.099. More micro-batches amortize the fixed 7-slot fill and drain.

question: In the Megatron MLP split, why is the first matmul column-parallel and the second row-parallel, rather than the reverse?
options: Column-first keeps the element-wise nonlinearity local; row-second gives partials one all-reduce sums
Because row-parallel matmuls run faster on GPUs, so the larger 4C-wide matmul should use them
Because the reverse order would need each device to hold twice as much weight memory overall
Because the reverse order changes the model's output, since ReLU does not commute with the split
explanation: If the first matmul were row-split, each device would get a partial pre-activation that must be summed before the nonlinearity, forcing a communication of the wide hidden layer. Column-then-row avoids that, needing only one all-reduce of the C-wide output.

question: What hardware does real tensor parallelism typically need, and what degree is common?
options: CPU clusters with many cores; degree equal to the number of cores per socket
GPUs across many nodes over standard Ethernet; a degree of 64 or more is typical
A single GPU with tensor cores, which split each matmul internally across units
GPUs on the fastest link (NVLink within a node); degree 2 to 8 is typical
explanation: Because it all-reduces on every layer's forward and backward, tensor parallelism needs the fastest interconnect, typically NVLink within one node. Degrees of 2 to 8 within a node are typical.

question: Why can pipeline parallelism span nodes over slower links?
options: It compresses activations to 1 bit before sending them across the node boundary
It does not communicate at all, since each stage owns its layers and its own data
Only activations cross stage boundaries, lighter than TP's per-layer all-reduces
It replicates every stage on every node, so traffic stays within each node's NVLink
explanation: Pipeline stages exchange only the activations (and their gradients) at stage boundaries, which is much less frequent than per-layer all-reduces. That makes pipeline parallelism tolerant of slower inter-node links, though it still needs many micro-batches.

question: Does model parallelism reduce the total compute needed to train a model?
options: No; it roughly doubles total compute, because every layer is recomputed across devices
Yes; splitting the matmuls halves the FLOPs per token compared with a single device
Yes; it divides the total compute by the number of GPUs used in the parallel layout
No; it makes a too-big model trainable and spreads the work, but total compute stays ~6ND
explanation: Training compute is about 6 times parameters times tokens regardless of how the work is split. Model parallelism spreads that compute and memory across devices so the model can be trained at all; it does not reduce the total.

question: After data parallelism, ZeRO/FSDP and tensor/pipeline/expert parallelism, what question do scaling laws address?
options: How to overlap each axis's communication with computation on a given cluster
How to split the matmuls across GPUs so that each one fits in device memory
How big to make the model and how much data to use for a given compute budget
How to route tokens to experts so the load stays balanced across devices
explanation: Parallelism is about how to train a given model fast. Scaling laws step back to ask how to choose model size and token count so that a compute budget yields the best model.
